why: Cousins are the nodes on the same level minus your siblings. A level-by-level BFS gives each level's total; each node's new value is that total minus the sum of its parent's children.
hints: The sum of a node's cousins equals the sum of its whole level minus the sum of itself and its sibling.
BFS level by level: first compute the level's total, then for each parent assign both of its children total - (left + right).

Here the tree is a level-order string array: rebuild child indices from it (each non-null node consumes the next two slots), run the BFS on indices, and write the new values back into the same positions. O(n).
pitfalls: Replacements are simultaneous: use original values, so compute all sums before overwriting.
The root and any only-child-level nodes with no cousins get 0.
Keep every 'null' marker in place in the output array.
In this level-order format, null entries do not reserve child slots; don't use the 2i+1 heap formula.
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds for practice:
  • 1 <= number of nodes <= 10^5
  • 1 <= node value <= 10^4
